practice.title: Perform a Gradient Descent Step
practice.taskOpening: Write step(fn): one descent step on the loss function it is handed. First define lossFn, a function of no arguments that returns the weight squared as a scalar. Then fill in step. Use tf.variableGrads(fn) for the slope rather than deriving it by hand: the whole point is that TFJS does the calculus for you. That call hands back an object of gradients keyed by variable name, so this weight's entry has to be pulled out of it and stored in gradient. Store the tensor itself, not a number read off it. Then update the weight by subtracting learningRate × gradient, and apply that with weight.assign so the tf.variable changes in place. Starting at weight = 5.0 with learningRate = 0.1, the first call lands the weight at exactly 4.0. The grader calls step() twice more on your loss, then three times on losses of its own: one of those is not a polynomial, and the last one is assembled while the grader runs, from a multiplier picked on the spot, so the body has to differentiate the function it receives instead of rebuilding the slope out of the loss value or repeating a number that was right on an earlier run. The grader also watches for the autograd call itself, and for what it was called on: a step that never runs the function it received through tf.variableGrads (or tf.grad) fails, whatever number it produced, so a differentiation call on some other function next to a slope worked out by hand does not count.

practice.title: Automatic Backpropagation
practice.taskOpening: Two ways to reach the same slope, and the exercise is the comparison between them. The starter declares the variable w at 3.0. (1) Write lossFn so it returns w squared. (2) Fill in gradOf(fn), which differentiates whatever loss function it is handed. It returns the loss the forward pass produced and, beside it, a gradient for every variable that loss touched, filed under the variable's own name. No derivative you worked out yourself appears anywhere in it. (3) Fill in numericGradOf(fn, variable), the estimate this lesson opens with, for one scalar variable at a time. Run fn at the variable's current value, run it again with that variable 0.001 higher, turn the difference into a slope, put the variable back, and return a plain number. The grader reassigns w and calls gradOf again, hands it two loss functions the exercise never shows you, the second over three variables at once, and checks that your two answers for it land within 0.05 of each other. It also counts how many times each of them runs the loss it was given, because that count is the difference between the two methods: the estimate pays a forward pass per variable, and the recorded pass pays one for all of them.

practice.title: Initialize TensorFlow.js
practice.taskOpening: Initialize TensorFlow.js, wait for it to be ready, and return an object containing the active backend name and TF.js version, shaped `{ backend, version }`. The request can fail two ways and neither is fatal: a registered backend that cannot start resolves false, and a name that was never registered throws, because its package was not imported. practice.title: Extract Fixed-Bin FFT Features
practice.taskOpening:
Build DEEP SCAN 2.0's input vector without the phase term. extractFeatures(signal, sampleRate, loHz, hiHz) returns one flat row. First the peak amplitude: the largest absolute sample value in the capture. Then the zero-crossing count: how many times consecutive samples land on opposite sides of zero. Then one FFT magnitude per fixed bin whose center falls inside the band from loHz to hiHz, endpoints included. Bin width is sampleRate divided by the number of samples, so 64 samples at 256 Hz gives 4 Hz bins and the 50 to 82 Hz band is bins 13 through 20. Leave the magnitudes in bin order. Sorting them by size would make the third feature mean a different frequency in every row. Report each magnitude at the height the transform gives it, unscaled: the normalization the lesson describes is measured across a whole training set and applied after extraction, not inside this function.
Here a crossing means strictly opposite signs on adjacent samples: one positive and one negative. A pair containing an exact zero contributes nothing. Other conventions exist; this exercise uses that one consistently.

practice.title: Simple Attention Over RNN Hidden States
practice.taskOpening:
Build `simpleAttention(query, keys, values)`. `query` is a rank-1 [d] vector: what this step is looking for. `keys` is [T, d], one key per time step, and a key exists only to be scored against the query. `values` is [T, dv], what a step hands over once it is selected, and dv does not have to equal d. Score every key against the query, softmax the scores into weights over the steps, then return the weighted sum of the VALUES as a rank-1 [dv] vector. Score with the raw dot product: no scaling. A production head divides the scores by the square root of the key width before the softmax, and this one does not, so the tests are pinned to the unscaled scores. Shape trap, called out up front: tf.matMul needs rank-2 inputs, and your query arrives rank-1, so reshape it to [1, d] on the way in and squeeze([0]) the [1, dv] result back to [dv] on the way out. Second trap: scoring a [1, d] query against [T, d] keys needs the keys transposed, because d has to face d. tf.matMul takes two booleans after the two tensors, transposeA and transposeB, and each transposes its own tensor before the multiply, so tf.matMul(q, k, false, true) does the same job as tf.matMul(q, k.transpose()) without building the transposed copy.
Remove only the batch axis. A value width of one must still return shape [1], not a scalar. The sequence is non-empty; for a single time step its position is 0.

practice.title: Implement a Kalman Filter
practice.taskOpening: Implement a simple 1D Kalman filter. The constructor is written for you, including the starting variance of 1. Write `update(measurement)`: one predict-correct step, returning the new estimate. Two fields carry state between calls and the tests read both, `this.estimate` and `this.variance`, so a correction has to write both. The weight the correction puts on the new measurement is not a constant you pick: it is built from the variance the filter is carrying when that measurement arrives, along with the two noise parameters, and the lesson's derivation drawer works out which value it has to be. Because it is rebuilt on every call it changes step to step, so an EMA with one fixed alpha fails the arithmetic tests. One test runs your filter across the falling pulse-interval log from the lesson and reads the gap between the final estimate and the final reading. A filter whose state is one number, with no term for change, trails a drifting signal instead of tracking it, and the test checks that your estimate lands on the trailing side.
